props.title: The Passion of Joan of Arc
props.initialSlug: Powerful religious drama with iconic performance

sections.content: Carl Theodor Dreyer's The Passion of Joan of Arc revolutionized cinematic close-ups and emotional intimacy. Renée Falconetti's haunting performance as Joan remains one of the most powerful in film history - her tear-streaked face and expressive eyes communicate more than pages of dialogue ever could. Dreyer's radical approach stripped away everything but the raw human elements, shooting mostly in tight close-ups at unusual angles. This technique influenced later masterpieces like Persona (1966) and The Trial of Joan of Arc (1962), showing how a face can become a landscape of human suffering and transcendence.

sections.content: The film's innovative cinematography by Rudolph Maté created a new visual language for depicting spiritual struggle. The harsh lighting, stark whites, and severe angles transform Joan's trial into an expressionist nightmare. This approach influenced religious cinema for decades, from The Seventh Seal (1957) to Breaking the Waves (1996). The deliberate lack of establishing shots and conventional coverage forces viewers into uncomfortable intimacy with Joan's suffering.

The film's restoration history adds another fascinating layer. The original negative was destroyed in a fire, and for decades, the film existed only in inferior copies. The 1981 discovery of a complete print in a Norwegian mental hospital janitor's closet reads like something from a thriller. This pristine copy allowed modern audiences to experience Dreyer's vision as intended, with the crystalline clarity of the original cinematography intact. SUBHEAD: Impact on Modern Cinema

sections.content: The film's influence extends far beyond religious or historical cinema. Its psychological intensity and unflinching close-ups echo in works like The Queen (2006) and First Reformed (2017). Modern directors like Paul Schrader and Lars von Trier have explicitly cited Dreyer's technique of using the human face as an emotional battleground. The film's approach to depicting interior spiritual struggles without supernatural elements set the template for serious religious filmmaking.
